title: Shakti as a philosophy
hook: a long hymn to the goddess opens with a sentence about a god who cannot even stir

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shakti as a philosophy began with Ramakrishna's snake: one snake, coiled or gliding, one reality at rest or at work. Did one busy moment look like power at work? Day one thousand eighty-two.

A long Sanskrit hymn to the goddess, the Saundarya Lahari, the wave of beauty, opens in a strange place. It doesn't begin with her face, or her weapons, or her lion. It begins with Shiva, the great god of the mountain, the destroyer, the lord of yogis. And in that first verse, what stands out is what he can't do. Without her, the verse says, he can't create. He can't even stir. Tradition says the hymn comes from Shankara, the teacher of non-duality. Whoever wrote it, they chose to start a praise of the goddess with a portrait of God standing perfectly still. Today: one verse, and the idea folded inside it.
screen: `THE WAVE OF BEAUTY.` → `IT OPENS WITH SHIVA.` → `WITHOUT HER, HE CAN'T STIR.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, in paraphrase. Shiva, when he is joined with Shakti, is able to create. If not, this god is not even able to move. So how could anyone without merit bow to you, or praise you, you who are worshipped by Vishnu, by Shiva, by Brahma? Listen to the play on words in the Sanskrit. Joined with shakti, power, Shiva becomes shakta, able. The verse sets the two sounds side by side, and the second time the sound means capable. Now turn it a second way. In the Puranas, Shiva and the goddess are a couple: Shiva and Parvati, married, with children. The verse doesn't deny that. But it says something sharper. She isn't only his wife. She is the reason anything he does gets done. Stillness on one side, movement on the other, and nothing happens until the two are together. A third way. The verse ends by saying the gods themselves worship her. Vishnu who protects, Brahma who creates, Shiva who dissolves: all of them, in this hymn, stand before her. Some who worship the goddess hear that line as the whole point. In their reading, power isn't a tool God picks up. It's the face of God that acts. And a fourth, smaller way in. Some readers hear the verse about ordinary life. A plan with no energy behind it sits on the table. A good intention that never moves is still just an intention. The verse is about God, but it's easy to see why people carry it home: stillness and power, the one who knows and the force that does.
screen: `JOINED WITH SHAKTI, SHIVA IS ABLE.` · `SHAKTI AND SHAKTA: POWER AND ABLE.` · `NOT ONLY HIS WIFE: HIS POWER TO ACT.` · `THE GODS THEMSELVES BOW TO HER.` · then, large: `WITHOUT HER, HE CANNOT EVEN STIR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: the plan and the stir. Sit, and let the breath settle. Bring to mind one thing you've been meaning to do and haven't started. Hold it as it is right now: a plan, sitting still on the table. Then, on each in-breath, picture the very first small step, the first word of the letter, the first number dialed. On each out-breath, let the picture rest. Don't do it yet. Just let the plan and the energy meet, again and again, the way the verse joins Shiva and Shakti. If you pray, you can hold the name Shakti, or Devi, or Ma, quietly with each breath out. If you don't, let the breath carry the plan. The bell holds the time.
Shakti as a philosophy. In the wave of beauty's opening verse, Shiva joined with Shakti is able to create. Without her, he cannot even stir.
Your line: Shakti as a philosophy. Today, pick one thing you've been meaning to do, a call, a letter, a walk, and give it the stir: start it, even for five minutes. Day one thousand eighty-two.

howItsDone: The Saundarya Lahari is chanted and studied by worshippers of the goddess, including in the Shri Vidya tradition, and a reading of it begins with this verse.

original.note: Sanskrit: shakti, power. In the verse, Shiva joined with shakti becomes shakta, able.

trapdoor: what you thought: Shakti is Shiva's wife.
what it means: in this hymn she is the power that lets God act at all. without her, Shiva cannot even stir.
what a scholar hears: śivaḥ śaktyā yukto yadi bhavati śaktaḥ prabhavitum: the verse plays śakti against śakta, able.

notes: Editor pass: review now picks up day 1081's snake and carry; hook no longer says the verse's 'very first thing' is what Shiva can't do (the verse opens with what he can do joined to Shakti); removed the 'one family of words' etymology line; 'for people who worship the goddess' softened to 'some who worship'; practice changed from body-stillness-watching-motion (repeated day 1074's practice) to a plan-and-stir practice. Checked against 1072–1081: Kali/Shiva stillness-and-power (1074) and Ramakrishna's snake (1081) are nearby but the verse angle is new.

Saundarya Lahari 1 paraphrased: śivaḥ śaktyā yukto yadi bhavati śaktaḥ prabhavituṃ / na ced evaṃ devo na khalu kuśalaḥ spanditum api / atas tvām ārādhyāṃ hari-hara-viriñcādibhir api / praṇantuṃ stotuṃ vā katham akṛta-puṇyaḥ prabhavati. 'Hari-Hara-Virinci' rendered as Vishnu, Shiva, Brahma: confirm that reading of Hara here (Shiva worshipping the goddess in the same verse that names him).
Authorship by Shankara given only as 'tradition says'; scholars debate it.
The śakti/śakta wordplay is presented as the verse's own, not as an etymology. The popular 'Shiva without i is shava' saying was deliberately left out.
howItsDone mentions Shri Vidya and that the first verse is 'often' recited at the start of a reading: Keeper to confirm or soften.
